title: 5 Ways to shock the muscle (GONE WRONG)
summary: He reviews the top Google result's five shock-the-muscle techniques. He ranks pre-exhaustion/activation highest, then increasing reps and training a muscle two days in a row; rest-pause and drop sets come last because of fatigue and lost intensity.
claims: Training a muscle two days in a row is valid: full recovery only matters for peak performance, not hypertrophy
Training before full recovery is not an exact science; beginners cannot judge it and pushing a partially recovered muscle can waste tonnage or cause injury
More advanced lifters can hit a muscle every 24 hours, such as a light blood-flow movement the day after a heavy lat day, for extra fiber damage
Evolving rep ranges progress through added reps and then added weight; 5x5 and 3x5 only progress by adding weight
Changing only reps and never weight, like staying at 225 on bench forever, also damages progress; you need both
Volume and intensity manipulation, not exercise changes, should be your first recourse against adaptation

Rest-pause keeps early mini-sets shy of failure, lets rest periods creep up for artificial performance gains, does not increase time under tension and leaks tonnage over time; extra sets are easier to track
Sets should end at or very close to muscular failure to be beneficial for hypertrophy
Rest-pause can work on some lifts, especially vertical presses
Drop sets train a fatigued muscle with submaximal loads, so use them only occasionally
Strength training for hypertrophy is monotonous; constantly chasing novelty or the pump gives poor results
He uses pre-exhaustion for chest but calls it activation: firing the muscle with a band improves performance, while hard cable isolation beforehand reduces it
Be careful supersetting with an already fatigued muscle that maintains mechanical integrity; you may hit mechanical failure sooner and get injured
His ranking: pre-exhaust first, increase reps second, train two days in a row third, rest-pause and drop sets tied last
